summary:
Nine evals were run (3 iterations each, 39 total runs, no failures). Five of the nine evals ("unrelated-*") were should_trigger:false checks — both variants correctly did NOT trigger the Firehose review skill on off-topic prompts (100% non-trigger pass rate for both), so these are negative controls with no quality/assertion data to compare.

The four substantive evals ("firehose-review-*") all confirmed the review skill fired as expected for both variants (3/3 trigger rate), but diverge sharply in whether the output met expectations:

- **firehose-review-trigger**: Both variants met expected output at the same rate (2/3, confidence medium for with_skill vs high for without_skill). At the assertion level, with_skill passed more checks overall (9/12 vs 6/12). Two checks ("frames as review" and "severity ratings present") passed for both every time — these aren't differentiating. Several others were flaky for both or favored with_skill (DataFreshness mention, scope-establishment, naming a severity level), and the "organized by Well-Architected pillar" check was flaky for both equally (1/2 each). Variant_a ran much longer (6m42s vs 2m50s) and cost more ($3.34 vs $1.41) for this eval. No quality-comparison pairs could be scored (all 3 skipped).

- **firehose-review-severity-definitions, firehose-review-http-endpoint-severity, firehose-review-pillars**: In all three, with_skill met the expected output 100% of the time (high confidence) and passed essentially every assertion (18/18, 15/15, 21/21 respectively), while without_skill met expected output 0% of the time and failed every corresponding assertion (0/12, 0/15, 0/7), also at high confidence — meaning this is a consistent, high-confidence gap rather than a borderline or noisy one. Variant_b was faster and cheaper in each of these (e.g., 1s/$0.01 vs 4s/$0.04; 8s/$0.07 vs 15s/$0.13; 0s/$0.00 vs 6s/$0.05), but the speed/cost advantage comes alongside a near-total miss on the expected content in these three evals. No quality-comparison pairs were scored for these either (all skipped), so independent quality judging is largely absent from this dataset.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) was only measured for two evals: in firehose-review-http-endpoint-severity, with_skill was rated fully "consistent" (score 3.0, high confidence) while without_skill was "mostly_consistent" (score 2.33, medium confidence); in firehose-review-pillars, only with_skill had a consistency rating ("mostly_consistent", 2.33) with no corresponding data for without_skill. These are limited data points, not comprehensive consistency profiles.

Overall picture: on three of four substantive evals, with_skill met the defined expected output far more often and passed far more assertions, consistently and at high confidence, while without_skill was faster and lower-cost but missed the targeted content in those same evals. On the fourth eval (firehose-review-trigger), the two were closer in expected-output rate but with_skill still edged out without_skill on raw assertion pass count, again while taking notably longer and costing more. No eval allowed a direct LLM-judged quality comparison (all quality-pairs were skipped across the board), so quality differences cannot be independently corroborated beyond the assertion-level pass/fail data, and the five unrelated/negative-control evals contribute no differentiating evidence at all.

firehose-review-trigger.summary:
This evaluation covered a single chat task (an Amazon Data Firehose operational/best-practices review) run 3 times per variant. The triggering behavior fired consistently for all runs (3/3), so the eval is a valid test of the scenario.

Expected output: Both variants met the expected output in 2 of 3 runs (67%), an identical rate. Confidence in this judgment was medium for with_skill and high for without_skill — not low, so the measurement itself is reasonably solid, though the sample is only 3 runs per variant, which limits how much weight either rate can bear.

Assertions (12 total per variant, from 6 distinct checks x 2 scored runs): with_skill passed 9/12 (75%) vs without_skill's 6/12 (50%). Breaking this down by individual assertion:
- Two assertions passed for both variants in all runs ("frames work as Firehose review" and "explicit severity rating per finding") — these aren't differentiating since both variants handle them equally well.
- One assertion ("organized by Well-Architected pillar") passed only half the time for both variants (flaky for both) — this suggests the assertion or underlying behavior is inconsistently met regardless of variant.
- Three assertions showed a split: "references DataFreshness/delivery-lag" (with_skill 2/2 vs without_skill 1/2), "asks for/establishes scope" (with_skill 1/2 vs without_skill 0/2), and "names a severity level" (with_skill 1/2 vs without_skill 0/2). On all three, with_skill passed more often than without_skill, though none were perfectly consistent (with_skill itself was not 2/2 on two of them), so these read as flaky-but-favoring-with_skill rather than clean passes.

Quality comparison: no quality pairs could actually be evaluated (0 evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no quality-based signal to weigh here — this dimension is simply absent data, not a tie or a loss for either side.

Runtime and cost: without_skill was substantially faster (avg 2m50s vs 6m42s) and cheaper (avg $1.41 vs $3.34) than with_skill. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (5.1% vs 6.7%), with no compaction events for either. Only one runtime pair was evaluated against the (very low) 30-second threshold, and that one run exceeded it — this threshold comparison has minimal sample size and should not be over-interpreted.

Output consistency: not available for either variant (null), so no conclusion can be drawn about run-to-run stability from this metric directly, though the flaky patterns seen in several assertions already hint at some output variability across runs for both variants.

Overall picture: with_skill passed more individual assertions and did somewhat better on a few specific checks (DataFreshness reference, scope-setting, naming severity levels), while matching without_skill exactly on overall expected-output rate (2/3 for both) and on the two assertions both variants handle well. Variant_a completed faster and at lower cost. No quality-comparison or consistency data exists to weigh against these differences, and several of the assertion differences stem from small samples (2 runs) with flaky (non-unanimous) results even within a single variant, so these differences should be read as directional signals rather than firm conclusions.

Both variants reliably triggered the behavior under test (3/3), so the test condition fired as expected for both. Beyond that, the two variants diverge sharply on this single chat eval, which asked for the five severity levels (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, INFO) presumably in order of urgency.

Expected-output match: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, also high confidence — so this is not a measurement-confidence issue, the judgment that without_skill failed is itself solid).

Per-assertion detail reinforces this: every one of the 6 distinct assertions (ordering of levels, and each of CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW/INFO being listed) shows the same pattern — with_skill passes consistently (3/3 each) and without_skill fails consistently (0/2 each, assertions evaluated on 2 of the 3 runs). There are no assertions where both variants pass, both fail, or where the pattern reverses — the split is uniform across all assertions in this eval, suggesting without_skill is missing or malforming the core content being tested (e.g., not listing all five levels or not providing them at all) rather than failing on some subtle edge case.

On cost and speed, without_skill was notably cheaper and faster (runtime ~1s, cost ~$0.01) compared to with_skill (~4s, ~$0.04), and both had low, non-compacted context utilization. However, given without_skill did not meet the expected output in any run, this speed/cost advantage comes alongside a complete failure to satisfy the task's correctness checks in this eval — a tradeoff only in the narrowest sense, since the faster/cheaper output did not deliver the expected content.

Quality comparison and output-consistency metrics were not available: all 3 quality pairs were skipped (0 evaluated), and output consistency is null for both variants, so no data exists on run-to-run stability or independent quality judgments beyond the assertion/expected-output checks. This eval covers only one task scenario (five severity levels), so these findings are based on a small sample (3 runs) and should be read as indicative of this specific scenario rather than a broad system-wide verdict.

firehose-review-http-endpoint-severity.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task (3 runs each) about classifying a Firehose HTTP endpoint destination check. The triggering condition for the test fired in all 3 runs (100%), so the behavior under test was reliably exercised for both variants.

On expected output and per-assertion results, there is a clear and consistent split: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, high confidence) and passed all 15 assertion instances (15/15, 100%). without_skill failed to meet the expected output in all 3 runs (0/3, high confidence) and failed every assertion instance (0/15, 0%). This pattern repeats identically across all 5 distinct assertions (covering severity classification as INFO, correct naming, the HTTPS-only endpoint reasoning, redirecting the check to key rotation/secure storage, and mentioning VPC/PrivateLink paths) — with_skill passed and without_skill failed on every one, with high confidence on both sides. Because every assertion shows the same pattern, this is a broad, consistent divergence rather than an isolated gap, but it also means none of the assertions differentiate finer-grained strengths/weaknesses — the signal is uniform across the board.

On efficiency metrics, without_skill was faster (8s vs 15s) and cheaper ($0.07 vs $0.13), with lower context window utilization (3.7% vs 6.0%); neither variant triggered any context compaction. So without_skill is more economical, but this comes alongside its complete failure to meet the expected output in this task.

Quality comparison data is not usable here: all 3 pairs were skipped and zero pairs were evaluated, so no direct quality judgment is available beyond the assertion/expected-output results above.

Output consistency was high for with_skill (rated "consistent" across all 3 dimensions, score 3.0, high confidence) and somewhat lower for without_skill ("mostly_consistent," score 2.33, with 1 consistent and 2 mostly-consistent dimensions, medium confidence) — indicating without_skill's outputs varied a bit more run-to-run, though this is a secondary signal given the confidence is only medium.

Overall, for this specific task, with_skill satisfied the expected behavior and all assertions while without_skill did not, consistently across all runs and at high confidence; without_skill's advantage was in lower runtime and cost, and quality-comparison data to cross-check this tradeoff was not available (all pairs skipped).

firehose-review-pillars.summary:
Both variants had the trigger behavior fire in all 3 test runs (3/3), so the test setup itself worked for both.

Beyond that, the two variants diverge sharply on this single chat eval, which asks about naming the seven AWS Well-Architected Framework pillars (security, reliability, performance, service quotas, cost optimization, operational excellence, sustainability):

- Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (3/3, 100%, high confidence). without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%, high confidence). Confidence in these judgments is high on both sides, so this is not a low-confidence artifact.
- Per-assertion results: with_skill passed all 21 assertion checks (21/21, 100%) and without_skill passed 0 of 7 (0/7, 0%). Looking at the per-assertion breakdown, every one of the 7 individual pillar-naming assertions shows the same pattern: with_skill passes and without_skill fails, consistently and with high confidence on both sides. There is no assertion that passed for both, failed for both, or showed a mixed/partial result — the pattern is uniform across all seven pillar checks.
- Metrics: with_skill had an average runtime of ~6s and average cost of ~$0.05, with low context-window utilization (5.6%) and no compaction. without_skill shows 0s runtime and $0.00 cost, with 3.6% context utilization — this near-zero runtime/cost combined with the 0/3 expected-output pass rate suggests without_skill may not have actually produced a substantive response in these runs, rather than simply being faster/cheaper.
- Quality comparison: no quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no direct quality judgment to weigh alongside the pass/fail data.
- Output consistency: with_skill was rated "mostly consistent" across runs (score 2.33, with 1 fully consistent and 2 mostly-consistent dimension ratings, high confidence). without_skill has no consistency rating (null), so nothing can be said about its run-to-run stability.

Overall, this eval shows a one-sided pattern favoring with_skill on every measured outcome (expected output, all 7 assertions, and consistency), with without_skill failing to meet the expected output or pass any assertions in any run. However, the quality comparison dimension is empty (skipped), and without_skill's near-zero runtime/cost raises the possibility that it did not generate a complete response for this task rather than reflecting a quality shortfall per se. These results come from a small sample (3 runs on one eval), so while the within-eval pattern is consistent and high-confidence, it reflects a single scenario rather than a broad performance picture.
